passage: Wednesday. At break, I saw Jatin sitting alone under the neem tree with his lunchbox closed. Everyone else was playing. I walked over. “Can I sit with you?” He shrugged, but he made room. I didn't say much. I opened my lunch and offered him a piece of my paratha. After a while, he said, “I miss my old school.” I said, “That sounds hard.” Then a group of boys came by and said something mean about his accent. I stood up and said, “Leave him alone.” They walked away, and I told Mrs. Rao what happened. Jatin looked at me and said thanks. Amandeep.

qa.q: Where was Jatin sitting alone?
qa.a: Under the neem tree.

qa.q: What was Jatin probably feeling when he sat with his lunchbox closed?
qa.a: He was probably lonely and missing his old school, which he said aloud after Amandeep sat with him.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do when the boys said something mean?
qa.a: Amandeep said “Leave him alone” and then told Mrs. Rao, so an adult knew.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt when the boys said something mean about Jatin's accent?
qa.a: Amandeep was probably protective of Jatin, standing up to say, "Leave him alone," and then telling Mrs. Rao.

grounding: A child sits with a lonely classmate and stands up for him, showing care, and also involves an adult.

passage: Under the peepal tree at the village school, Farida sat by herself with her knees drawn up, because the girls had left her out of the skipping rope game. Deepika saw her and stopped playing. She came over with two guavas from her bag and sat beside Farida. “Want one?” Farida took it without a word. Deepika ate hers, then said, “Come and jump with me.” Farida shook her head, so Deepika stayed where she was, and the two of them watched the rope from the shade. After a few minutes Farida stood up. “Okay, my turn next,” she said. Deepika grinned.

qa.q: How many guavas did Deepika bring?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: What did Deepika's choice to stay beside Farida show about what she wanted?
qa.a: She wanted Farida to feel less alone, and staying without pushing showed care and respect for Farida's feelings.

qa.q: What helped Farida rejoin the game?
qa.a: Deepika sat with her, shared a guava and did not force her, and after a few minutes Farida chose to stand up.

qa.q: How might Farida have felt when the girls left her out?
qa.a: Farida probably felt lonely and hurt, since she sat by herself with her knees drawn up.

grounding: A child sits with a lonely classmate to show care and solidarity, without pressuring her to join.

passage: In the Lisbon school canteen, Abebe sat alone every day with his injera wrapped in foil. On Thursday, two boys walked past and held their noses. Paulo, at the next table, watched Abebe's shoulders curl. He picked up his tray and sat down opposite him. “What's that? It looks like a pancake.” Abebe blinked, then tore off a piece. “Injera. Try.” Paulo did. “It's sour! I like it.” When the two boys came back and started again, Paulo stood up. “Stop it. It's just food.” Then he walked to the lunch supervisor and told her. She came over, spoke to the boys and later told Paulo, “That was brave, and telling me was the right move.”

qa.q: What was Abebe's lunch wrapped in?
qa.a: His injera was wrapped in foil.

qa.q: What was Abebe feeling when the boys held their noses?
qa.a: Abebe felt hurt and embarrassed, his shoulders curling as they mocked his food.

qa.q: Which of Paulo's actions showed solidarity, and why was telling the supervisor right?
qa.a: Sitting with Abebe and standing up to the boys showed care, and telling the supervisor brought in an adult who could stop the teasing.

qa.q: How did the lunch supervisor respond?
qa.a: She spoke to the boys and praised Paulo for being brave and for telling her.

grounding: Shows a child sitting with a lonely classmate and standing up for him, and involving an adult, which the adult praises.

passage: In the first week at the residential school, Jyoti sat alone on the dining-hall steps every evening, not eating. Siddharth noticed on Monday, and again on Tuesday. On Wednesday he brought two bananas and sat a step below her. “Want one?” She shook her head, then took it. They didn't talk much. He told her about the hostel cat, and she almost smiled. On Thursday she still hadn't eaten dinner. Siddharth felt uneasy. This was more than he could fix with bananas. He went to the house warden and told her. The warden thanked him, sat with Jyoti that evening and called her parents. Later she told Siddharth, “You were a good friend, twice.”

qa.q: What did Siddharth bring on Wednesday?
qa.a: Siddharth brought two bananas.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when Jyoti still hadn't eaten on Thursday?
qa.a: Siddharth felt uneasy and worried, sensing the problem was bigger than he could fix alone.

qa.q: Why was going to the warden the right step?
qa.a: Jyoti not eating for days needed an adult's help, and the warden sat with her and called her parents that evening.

qa.q: What did the warden mean by “a good friend, twice”?
qa.a: The warden meant Siddharth helped once by sitting with Jyoti and again by telling an adult when it became serious.

grounding: Shows a child sitting with a lonely classmate and knowing when to involve an adult, with the adult praising both.

passage: I'm Charu. At the bus stop on Friday, two older boys started shoving Kunal, snatching his cap and throwing it between them. Kunal's face went white. Most of us looked away. Vijay didn't. He walked right up, not fast, and stood next to Kunal. “Give it back. Come on, Kunal, stand with me.” The older boys laughed but tossed the cap on the ground. Then Vijay did something I didn't expect: he didn't shout or push. He took Kunal straight to the teacher on bus duty and told her everything. She wrote down the boys' names and called both their homes that evening. I don't know what Vijay was feeling. His hands were shaking a bit.

qa.q: What did the older boys snatch from Kunal?
qa.a: They snatched Kunal's cap.

qa.q: What might Vijay have been feeling as he stood next to Kunal?
qa.a: Vijay was probably scared, his hands shaking a bit, but determined to stand up for his friend.

qa.q: What made Vijay's response safe and wise?
qa.a: He stood beside Kunal without fighting, then took him straight to the teacher on duty, who acted that evening.

qa.q: How did most of the other children react?
qa.a: Most of them, Charu included, looked away, which made Vijay's step stand out.

grounding: Shows a child standing up for a friend and involving an adult when the situation is unsafe.

passage:
Monday: Tarun, new from Bihar, ate his lunch alone on the steps again. Sachin picked up his tiffin and sat beside him. "Is that litti? My Nani makes it." Tarun's face opened like a window.

Wednesday: Near the cycle stand, two Class 8 boys grabbed Tarun's cap and held it high. "Say please in Bhojpuri!" Sachin stepped in. "Give it back." One shoved him hard. Sachin didn't shove back. He ran straight to the PT teacher, Mr Sequeira, who came at once, got the cap back and took both boys to the office.

Friday: In assembly, Mr Sequeira said, "Standing by a friend is brave. Getting an adult when it turns rough is braver still." Sachin and Tarun, sharing a bench, tried not to grin.

qa.q: What was Tarun eating on Monday?
qa.a: Litti.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when Sachin sat beside him on Monday?
qa.a: Relieved and happy to have company after eating alone, and less lonely as a newcomer.

qa.q: Why was running to Mr Sequeira the right move on Wednesday?
qa.a: Once the older boys shoved him, it was unsafe to handle alone; fetching the PT teacher protected both boys and got the cap back.

qa.q: How did Mr Sequeira view Sachin's actions?
qa.a: He saw both standing by a friend and fetching an adult as brave, and praised fetching an adult as braver still.

grounding: It shows a child sitting with a lonely classmate and standing up for him, then getting an adult when it turns unsafe, and being praised for both.
